text.p: Singapore and Malaysia, their fragile ties in the spotlight on Thursday, have been closely linked since the birth of a British settlement on the island at the foot of the Malaysian peninsula in 1819.

Malaysian newspapers quoted unidentified ministers as saying after a cabinet meeting on Wednesday that fresh initiatives with Singapore would be suspended, including new contracts to Singaporean companies.
Malaysia on Thursday denied it had frozen ties.
Both were a part of the post-British colonial Federation of Malaya from 1963 to 1965 before Singapore was asked to leave over deep political differences about its future direction.
Despite the divorce, the two countries remain highly dependent on each other.
Following are some of the main links:

* ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations which also includes Brunei, Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam. The 30-year-old grouping has grown into one of the world's most economically dynamic regions. Its leaders meet regularly and have lengthy informal talks.
* Both have populations made up largely of Malays, ethnic Chinese and ethnic Indians. Malaysia has a majority of Malays and Singapore a majority of ethnic Chinese.
* Physically, the two countries are linked by a colonial era causeway. Malaysia has proposed building a bridge to replace it. Singapore has said it would look favourably on the idea.
* On an average weekend, 100,000 Singaporeans cross the causeway to Malaysia. Singapore's population is 2.8 million.
* Much of Singapore's food and most of its water comes from Malaysia, which is also among the five main suppliers of oil to Singapore's big refining industry.
* Trade between them is huge. Two-way trade was worth $3.74 billion in January alone.
* Singapore has huge investments in Malaysia. Last year it pumped in $1.3 billion and was the biggest foreign investor.

* Malaysian companies ship goods worth around US$5.14 through Singapore a year. In 1995, the last year for which figures are available, about a quarter of Malaysia's overseas trade passed through Singapore.
* Some 129 Malaysian stocks are traded over the counter in Singapore.
